content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe how concentration affects reaction rate
Explain the effect using collision theory
Design experiments to investigate concentration effects

is one of the key factors affecting reaction rate. Increasing the concentration of reactants generally increases the rate of reaction. This principle is used extensively in industry and the laboratory.
Increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction.
More concentrated solutions contain more particles in the same volume
More particles = more collisions = faster rate
[DIAGRAM: Two beakers - dilute solution (few particles) vs concentrated solution (many particles)]
Higher concentration = more reactant particles per unit volume
Particles are closer together on average
This increases the frequency of collisions
More collisions per second means more successful collisions per second
Therefore, the rate of reaction increases
Volume of gas vs time at different concentrations:
All lines reach the same final volume
if same amount of limiting reactant
Investigating Concentration - Marble Chips and Acid
Dependent variable: Volume of CO₂ produced (or mass lost)
Control variables: Mass of marble chips, surface area, temperature, volume of acid
Set up gas syringe or balance
Add 50 cm³ of 0.5 M HCl to flask
Start timer and record gas volume every 30 s
Repeat with 1.0 M, 1.5 M, and 2.0 M HCl
Higher concentration → steeper curve → faster rate
All reach same final volume (same mass of CaCO₃)
Place flask on paper with black cross
Add 50 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution
Add 5 cm³ of dilute HCl and start timer
Repeat with different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate
Keep total volume constant by adding water
Higher concentration = shorter time = faster rate
If concentration doubles, rate approximately doubles.
(Often gives a straight line through the origin for simple reactions)
Explain, using collision theory, why doubling the concentration of hydrochloric acid approximately doubles the rate of reaction with magnesium.
Doubling concentration means twice as many HCl particles per unit volume
The particles are on average closer together
There are twice as many collisions per second
Twice as many successful collisions occur per second

What pattern do the results show?
Rate is directly proportional to concentration
In an experiment, 2M acid produced 50 cm³ of gas in 20 seconds. Predict approximately how long it would take 1M acid to produce 50 cm³ of gas.
Half the rate means twice the time for the same amount of product
Thinking higher concentration produces more product
Higher concentration produces product FASTER, not more (total product depends on amount of reactant)
Not keeping total volume constant when diluting
Add water to maintain constant volume when comparing concentrations
Only change concentration; keep surface area, temperature, etc. constant
More particles per volume → more collisions → more successful collisions
On graphs: higher concentration = steeper initial gradient
All lines reach same final value (same limiting reactant)
Rate is often proportional to concentration (Rate ∝ [reactant])
